Yes. The subtext enriches the story’s setting and social dynamics rather than feeling forced. Miss Emily’s correction of Marnie’s “ain’t” appears helpful but implicitly polices class boundaries, while her praise of “those girls” both recognizes Marnie’s ability and keeps her socially subordinate. These exchanges make Laurel Ridge’s restrained atmosphere feel quietly controlling.

The recurring ring also carries meaning beyond its literal value: Marnie’s final decision to turn it outward suggests growing confidence in her new position, without entirely resolving the compromises that accompany it. These implications emerge naturally through dialogue, gestures, and objects.
